description: How SAS computes percentiles/quantiles (default PCTLDEF=5) and why it differs from numpy/pandas defaults.

pctldef5_default.title: SAS default percentiles use PCTLDEF=5 (averaged empirical CDF), not linear interpolation.
rule: SAS PROC MEANS/SUMMARY/UNIVARIATE default to PCTLDEF=5, the 'averaged empirical distribution function' definition.
For a percentile p (0-100) over n non-missing sorted values y[1..n]: let j = n * (p/100).
- If j is an integer, the percentile is the average of the j-th and (j+1)-th order statistics: (y[j] + y[j+1]) / 2.
- Otherwise it is the ceil(j)-th order statistic: y[ceil(j)].
numpy.percentile / pandas.quantile default to method='linear' (Hyndman-Fan type 7), which interpolates and gives DIFFERENT results, especially for small n.
To match a SAS baseline exactly, implement PCTLDEF=5 explicitly rather than calling numpy defaults.
pitfalls: Using np.percentile(x, 25) or df.quantile(0.25) will silently mismatch SAS on small groups.
Missing values must be dropped before computing order statistics (SAS ignores missing in percentile stats).
Percentiles are 1-indexed on the sorted order statistics; guard the index into [1, n].

code: if k == j and 0 < k < n:          # j is an integer -> average two order stats
